title: A ready-built truck for your agent

beats.say: Would you build a whole truck just to deliver one sofa?

show.text: Build a truck for one sofa?
show.sub: Or just drive one that exists

beats.say: Writing an AI agent by hand is like that. You code the loop that asks the model, runs a tool, and feeds back the answer. Then you still need brakes, mirrors and a horn.

The Claude Agent SDK is the truck, already built. An SDK is just a toolkit you install into your own program. This one is the same engine that powers Claude Code. It already reads files, searches, and runs commands, with safety rules.
You only choose the cargo and the route: your own tools, and your own rules.

check.q: Why use the Agent SDK instead of hand-writing an agent loop?
opts: It removes the need for any model
It gives you a tested harness so you focus on tools and rules
It makes the agent free to run
check.why: The SDK supplies the loop, built-in tools and permissions that already power Claude Code. You still pay for the model and still define your own tools and rules.

work: List the parts of your current agent loop that are plumbing rather than business logic.
Name the one custom tool your agent would need that no built-in tool covers.

title: What one install gives you

beats.say: What do you actually get when you install one package?
Run pip install claude agent sdk. Set your Anthropic API key as an environment variable, never in the code, because code gets committed and shared. Bedrock or Vertex also work.

Your Python program then hands the harness a prompt. The harness runs the loop: the model picks a tool such as Read, Grep, Bash or Edit, the harness checks permissions, runs it, and returns the result. It also trims context so long jobs do not overflow.
You add custom tools, MCP servers and subagents. Your effort goes to tools, guardrails and evaluation, not plumbing.

check.q: Where should the Anthropic API key live?
opts: Hard-coded in the agent script
In an environment variable
In the system prompt
check.why: Code is committed and shared, so a key in it leaks. An environment variable keeps the secret outside the repository.

work: Set the API key through your secrets manager or environment, and scan your repo for hard-coded keys.
Run a tiny prompt through the SDK and watch which built-in tools the model picks.

title: Gotchas of a powerful harness

beats.say: What stops a coding agent from deleting the wrong folder?

Nothing, unless you set rules. The built-in Bash and Edit tools act on the real machine with your process's access. So the permissions layer matters: allow only the tools the job needs, and ask or deny for the risky ones.

chip.text: Allow only what the job needs

beats.say: Second gotcha: every loop turn is a paid model call. A confused agent can circle for dozens of turns, so cap the turns and watch spend. Third, a leaked key is a leaked bill. Keep the API key in the environment, and never print it in logs.

show.title: Failure modes
items: Runaway turns cost money: cap them
Secrets stay out of logs and code

beats.say: Test with evaluations, because the same prompt can take different paths each run.

show.sub: So evaluate, do not just demo

check.q: An agent keeps retrying a failing task for 40 turns. What is the best control?
opts: Give it more tools
Cap the turns and monitor spend
Hide the errors from the model
check.why: Each turn is a paid model call, so a turn limit and spend monitoring bound the cost of a stuck loop.

work: Define an explicit allow list of tools for each agent and deny shell access by default.
Set a maximum turn count and alert on unusual spend.
Build a small evaluation set to catch behavior changes between runs.

title: Harness, workflow, or your own loop

beats.say: When is a battle-tested agent harness the wrong choice?

If the task is a fixed pipeline, say classify a ticket then fill a form, a plain model call or a simple workflow is cheaper, faster and easier to predict. An agent loop adds turns, latency and variance you may not need.

Use the SDK when the path is open-ended, like debugging a repo. Then you inherit tested tools and context handling, and you couple to one vendor's harness. Run it inside a sandboxed container, so the blast radius stays small.
Choose by predictability: fixed steps get a workflow, open-ended work gets the harness, and exotic loop control justifies your own.

check.q: Which task best justifies using the Agent SDK harness?
opts: Classify each support ticket into one of five labels
Investigate and fix a failing test across an unfamiliar repo
Translate a paragraph into French
check.why: Open-ended work needs the model to choose tools and steps, which the harness handles. The other two are fixed, single-call tasks.

work: Classify your agent use cases as fixed pipeline or open-ended, and move the fixed ones to plain workflows.
Run any SDK agent in a sandboxed container with minimal file and network access.

title: A toolbox for a smart new hire

beats.say: What if your AI assistant could look up your company's real numbers, instead of guessing?

show.sub: Custom tools let the AI look

beats.say: Think of a new employee on day one. They are smart, but they do not know where anything is. So you hand them a labelled toolbox. One button says, show revenue by country.
A custom tool is exactly that button. You write a small function, and give it a clear name and a plain description. The assistant reads the label, decides when to press it, and gets an answer back.
Good labels matter. A vague label means the button gets pressed wrongly, or never. Keep each button small, and safe to press: look, but do not change.

check.q: Why does the description of a custom tool matter so much?
opts: It makes the function run faster
The assistant reads it to decide when to use the tool
It is required to connect to the database
It encrypts the results
check.why: The model never sees your code. It only sees the name and description, so a vague label leads to wrong or missed tool calls.

work: Write a one-sentence description for each tool and ask a colleague if they would know when to use it.
List the three questions people ask your data team most, and make each a candidate tool.

title: From Python function to callable tool

beats.say: How does a plain Python function become something Claude can call?
You decorate it with tool. Three things go in: a name, a description, and an input schema. Here the schema is empty, because revenue by country needs no arguments.

show.title: The decorator
show.text:
@tool("revenue_by_country",
  "Revenue and order count per country",
  {})
async def revenue_by_country(args): ...

beats.say: Then create sdk mcp server wraps your tools into a server that runs inside your own program. There is no separate process and no network hop.
In the options, you register the server under dq, and list the allowed tools. The full name is mcp, double underscore, dq, double underscore, revenue by country. Max turns of ten caps the loop.

check.q: What does the allowed tools list need to contain for the agent to use your tool?
opts: The Python function name only
The full name, mcp then server name then tool name
Nothing, all tools are always allowed
The database path
check.why: Tools from an MCP server are named with the mcp prefix, the server name and the tool name. A wrong name means the tool is not permitted.

work: Turn one existing SQL query into a tool and register it under a named server.
Set max turns on every agent so a confused loop ends quickly.

title: Why a working tool still fails

beats.say: Your tool returned data. So why did the agent still get it wrong?
The result must be a dictionary with a content list holding text blocks. Return a bare list and the call breaks. Our example dumps the rows as JSON text inside one block.

Failures matter too. If the query throws, the agent learns nothing useful. Catch the error and return a short message saying what went wrong and what to try. The agent can then retry or change course.
Also watch size. Dump a million rows and you burn the context window. Return aggregates, or cap rows at fifty. And open the database read only, as the example does, so a mistake cannot write.

check.q: A tool query raises an exception. What is the best behaviour?
opts: Let it crash the whole agent
Return an empty list silently
Return a short message explaining the failure and what to try
Retry forever inside the tool
check.why: A clear message lets the model adjust its next step. Silence hides the problem and a crash ends the run.

work: Wrap each tool body in error handling that returns a readable message.
Add a row cap and test with your biggest table.

title: Which tools to build, and where to run them

beats.say: Should every data source become a custom tool?
In-process tools are fast and simple, with nothing to deploy. But they live and die with your agent process, and share its credentials. That is fine for one team, awkward for ten.
When many agents need the same tools, run a standalone MCP server. You get one place for authentication, audit logs and versioning.

Also, prefer a few narrow, read-only tools over one tool that runs any SQL. Free-form SQL is flexible, but it is a security hole and a cost risk. Fewer, sharper tools also help the model choose correctly.

check.q: Five different agents need the same warehouse tools. What is the best choice?
opts: Copy the tool code into each agent
Give each agent a tool that runs any SQL
Host one shared MCP server with auth and audit logs
Remove the tools and paste data into prompts
check.why: A shared server centralises credentials, logging and versions, so fixes and access control happen in one place.

work: Audit your tools and replace any run-any-SQL tool with narrow, named ones.
Decide a threshold, such as three agents, after which a tool moves to a shared server.

title: One call, like briefing an assistant

beats.say: Imagine handing a question to a careful assistant. They walk off, read your files, and come back with an answer. Could software do that?

show.sub: An agent works through files for you

beats.say: That is one call to an agent. You give it the question: why are amounts too high. You give it a rulebook: it may only look at files, never change them. You cap it at eight steps, so it cannot wander forever. And a house rule: show your evidence.
Then it works, and reports back as it goes: what it is thinking, which file it opened. The very last note is the bill, showing what the whole job cost. Read that every time.

check.q: In the analogy, why do you cap the assistant at eight steps?
opts: So it cannot wander forever and run up cost
So it answers faster than a person
So it can change files safely
So it forgets the question
check.why: A turn limit bounds how long and how costly one job can get. It does not make the work faster or safer on its own.

work: Write down, for one real question, what the agent may read and what it must never touch.
Pick a step cap before you run anything, not after a surprise bill.

title: Anatomy of a query call

beats.say: What actually happens when you call query, and why do you loop over it with async for?

show.sub: returns a stream, not one answer

beats.say: You pass a prompt and an options object. The options set the folder, three read-only tools, eight turns at most, the model, and a system prompt. A turn is one round of the model thinking, then maybe using a tool.

The call does not return one answer. It returns a stream. Each message arrives as soon as it exists: assistant text, a tool request, a tool result. That way you watch a long job live instead of waiting blind.
The final message is the result. It holds total cost and token usage. Log it every run, or you cannot say what an answer cost.

check.q: Why is query consumed with async for?
opts: It returns a stream of messages as work happens
It runs eight copies in parallel
It only works inside a database
It hides the cost from you
check.why: The agent produces many messages over time. Streaming lets you see progress and read the final result message at the end.

work: Run the example and print only the message types, to learn the stream's shape.
Save the cost and token usage from the result message into a run log.

title: Gotchas around the stream

beats.say: Your agent hit eight turns and stopped mid-thought. What did you get back?

show.sub: and the answer is not done

beats.say: Still a result message, but flagged as an error, with a subtype saying max turns was reached. Your code must check that, not assume the last text is the answer. Treat it like a timeout.

show.title: Limit hit is a *result*, not a crash

beats.say: Second gotcha: allowed tools is a pre-approval list. It says what runs without asking. To truly forbid a tool, use the disallowed list too. And the working folder sets where relative paths start. It is not a security sandbox.

show.title: Permissions are not walls
items: Allowed tools means pre-approved, not the only ones
Use the disallowed list to block a tool
The working folder is a starting point, not a sandbox

beats.say: Third: cost arrives only in the last message. If you break out of the loop early or crash, you lose the bill. Write what you have in a finally block.

check.q: You list only Read, Grep and Glob in allowed tools. What is the safest extra step to make sure no write tool runs?
opts: Nothing, the list already blocks all others
Also put write tools in the disallowed list
Raise max turns
Change the model
check.why: Allowed tools pre-approves; it does not by itself forbid others. The disallowed list is the explicit block.

work: Test a run with max turns set to 1 and confirm your code handles the error result.
Wrap the loop so the cost is logged even if the loop exits early.

title: When a single agent call is wrong

beats.say: When is an agent call the wrong tool for a data question?
Cost grows faster than turns. Each turn re-reads the whole conversation so far, so eight turns with big files can cost many times one prompt. Caching helps, but cap turns and track cost per run.

If the question repeats, like total amounts by country, write a SQL check or a test. It is cheaper, repeatable, and reviewable. Use the agent for open questions, like why, where nobody knows which file to read.

Match the model to the job: a small model for searching, a larger one for reasoning. For follow-up questions, move from one-shot query to a session client. And run it in a sandbox, since prompts can be tricked.

show.title: Design choices
items: Small model to search, larger model to reason
Sandbox plus read-only tools for untrusted input

check.q: A team asks the same question, total amounts by country, every morning. What do you choose?
opts: An agent call with eight turns each day
A scheduled SQL check with a test
A larger model
A session client
check.why: A repeating, well-defined question is cheaper, exact and reviewable as SQL or a test. Agents suit open-ended investigation.

work: Review your agent runs and move any repeating question into SQL or a test.
Set a per-run cost alert from the logged result messages.

title: The intern with the keys

beats.say: Would you give a brand new intern every key in the building, and then never check their work?
Of course not. You would hand over only the keys they need. You would set a time limit and a spending limit. And you would ask for a standard form, not a rambling story.
Then you would test them on a practice case where you already know the answer. You would keep a logbook. And before they change anything important, a manager signs off.
An AI agent that runs every night needs exactly the same care. A demo works once, while you watch. Production runs at three in the morning, when nobody is looking.

check.q: Why give a nightly agent only the tools it needs?
opts: It makes the agent faster at thinking
If it goes wrong, the damage it can do is small
It lowers the price of each word it writes
check.why: Least privilege limits the blast radius. A mistaken or confused agent can only touch what you allowed.

work: List every tool your agent has and remove any it never uses.
Ask yourself what the worst thing is that this agent could do tonight.

title: Limits, schema and logs

beats.say: How do you stop a nightly agent from looping for an hour and burning fifty dollars?

First, limits. Set max turns to fifteen, a budget of one dollar, and a timeout of five minutes. If three turns pass with no new finding, stop. Second, least privilege: allow read-only query tools, and leave Bash out.

Third, structured output. Make the agent return a schema with severity, findings and evidence. Your pipeline can validate it, reject bad shapes, and page someone on high severity. Code cannot check prose.
Finally, log every run: prompt version, tool calls, cost and outcome. Then you can answer what changed last Tuesday.

check.q: What is the main benefit of a schema for the agent's output?
opts: Other code can validate and route it automatically
The agent needs fewer tokens to think
It guarantees every finding is true
check.why: A schema lets your system check the shape and act on fields like severity. It does not prove the content is correct.

work: Set max_turns, a dollar cap and a timeout on your agent today.
Define a findings schema with severity and evidence fields.

title: Evals and hidden gotchas

beats.say: You changed one line in the prompt. Did the agent get better or worse?
Build a small set of cases with known answers. Inject a duplicate order into a test table and check the agent finds it. Add a clean table too, to catch false alarms.
Run them on every change to the prompt, tools or model. Models vary between runs, so run each case several times and read the pass rate, not one result.
Gotchas. A valid schema does not mean true findings, so demand evidence like row ids and check them. Read-only access can still leak customer data into logs, so redact them.

show.title: Gotchas
items: Valid shape is not true content
Check evidence such as row ids

check.q: Why run each eval case several times?
opts: The first run is always cached
Agent output varies, so one result can mislead
It makes the budget limit reset
check.why: Model output is not deterministic. A pass rate across repeats shows whether a change really helped.

work: Create five eval cases, including one clean case with nothing to find.
Run the set on every prompt, tool or model change and record the pass rate.

title: Should it even be an agent?

beats.say: Before you harden an agent, ask: should this task be an agent at all?
If the steps are fixed, a plain SQL test is cheaper, faster, and gives the same answer every time. Use an agent only where the investigation path varies, like explaining why a number moved.
Cost is runs times turns times context. At fifty cents a run across two hundred tables, that is one hundred dollars a night. Triage with a cheap model, and send only hard cases to a stronger one.
Keep actions gated: the agent recommends, a pipeline with tests applies. Autonomy is earned by weeks of passing evals, not granted by one good demo.

check.q: A check always follows the same three steps. What fits best?
opts: An agent with a large budget
A deterministic SQL or pipeline test
An agent with Bash access
check.why: Fixed logic is cheaper, faster and repeatable as plain code. Agents earn their cost only when the path varies.

work: Review your agent tasks and move any fixed-step ones to plain tests.
Estimate nightly cost as runs times average cost, and set an alert on it.
